findings.summary: The round-2 major (ownerless obligation) was swept from the two src/main javadocs but NOT from the M5.41 status cell, whose last sentence still assigns the wiring to M5.45b and to M5.13/M5.14 -- two DONE rows -- and thereby contradicts M5.58 and both repointed javadocs inside the same commit
findings.detail: Verified against the tree, not against prose. M5.41's status cell says two sentences apart: (a) 'IT HAD NO OWNER IN ROUND 2 and review caught that: M5.13, M5.14 and M5.41 are all done, so naming them left it with nobody', and (b) 'Wiring the hub to the new overload is M5.45b's and M5.13/M5.14's, which is where a blocking sink first becomes reachable'. Sentence (b) is the exact claim round 2 raised as M5.41-3 and is the sentence the SegmentProxy javadoc was CHANGED to stop saying ('M5.58 owns it -- M5.13, M5.14 and M5.41 are all done, so naming them would have left the obligation with nobody'). Confirmed statuses: M5.13 done (commit f145c51 lineage, row ends 'NOT WIRED ... M5.43'), M5.14 done, M5.45b 'blocked -- M5.43' and scoped to `direct`, not to the proxy fan-out. It is minor and not major only because the obligation now genuinely HAS an owner and three of four pointers are right: M5.58's row states the prohibition in its first clause, SegmentProxy.java:118 and :198-203 both name M5.58, and SubscriptionHub.java:403 names M5.58. The wrong pointer survives in a DONE row's retrospective narrative, which is not where a taker is assigned work. It is the 'contract prose restated everywhere' pattern: the claim lived in three places and the fix reached two.
findings.failure_scenario: An agent picks up M5.45b (direct serving) and, per its dependency chain, reads M5.41's done row to learn what the proxy path now guarantees. The cell tells it wiring the three-argument overload is M5.45b's own work. It wires SubscriptionHub.streamFromStore to the deadline overload without the return-shape change, because the row it is holding says the job is its. SubscriptionHub.java:443 then reaches `if (sink.failed)` for a sink that TIMED OUT -- Tracking sets `failed` only in the catch at :525, a dropped sink never throws -- so :447 calls `subscriber.complete(...)` on a consumer holding a truncated prefix it cannot tell from a whole segment. That is precisely the failure chain M5.41 exists to remove. The one-line close is to cut 'and M5.13/M5.14's' or replace the clause with M5.58; review.md rule 11 says leaving it and recording it is the usual right call, since the next round's surface is the prose the fix adds.

findings.summary: The new `@throws IOException` tag says the interrupt is 'the one case where this differs from the two-argument method'; there are at least two further differences, one of them behavioural rather than a throws contract
findings.detail: The clause is scoped inside `@throws IOException`, so the charitable reading is 'the one case where the IOException contract differs', and under that reading it is true. Read as written it over-claims. The other differences: (1) the three-argument overload throws IllegalArgumentException for a non-positive deadline -- documented one tag below, so a reader sees the contradiction immediately; (2) more substantively, the two-argument method calls `SegmentSink.write` on the CALLER's thread, while handOff submits one virtual thread per sink per chunk, so a sink is entered by a different thread on every chunk. SegmentSink's javadoc states no thread-affinity contract, so nothing is violated, and a happens-before chain does exist (task completion -> invokeAll return -> main thread submits the next chunk), so no visibility bug follows. But a sink holding a non-reentrant lock across chunks, a ThreadLocal, an MDC, or an event-loop affinity assertion behaves differently under the two overloads, and 'the one case where this differs' tells a sink author it does not.
findings.failure_scenario: Whoever takes M5.58 reads this @throws tag to decide what changes when the hub is repointed at the deadline overload, concludes the only behavioural delta is an interrupt path, and repoints it. SubscriptionHub.Tracking.failed (SubscriptionHub.java:514) is a plain non-volatile boolean written inside `write`; under the two-argument method it is written and read by one thread, under the three-argument one it is written by a virtual worker and read by the serving thread at :443. The invokeAll happens-before chain does in fact carry it, so this does not fail today -- but the reasoning that it is safe is not available to a reader the tag has told there is nothing thread-shaped to check. Cheapest close is two words: 'the one case where the IOException CONTRACT differs', plus one sentence in the handOff javadoc saying write is now entered on a per-chunk virtual thread.

findings.summary: The narrowed buffer-race paragraph is TRUE, but the exception it records is stated only in SegmentProxy; SegmentSink still tells a sink author that the bytes are valid for the duration of the call, which stops being true for a dropped sink under the new overload
findings.detail: The narrowing itself checks out and I verified it rather than accepting it: invokeAll(tasks, timeout, unit) returns only when every returned Future isDone(); tookIt keeps a sink only when !isCancelled() and get() returns normally, which means that task's `write` returned before invokeAll returned; so at the moment `in.read(buffer)` refills the array for the next chunk, every sink still in `live` has provably left write, and only a cancelled -- i.e. dropped -- task can still hold the reference. 'ONLY a dropped one' is correct. What is not stated where a sink author reads it: SegmentSink's class javadoc says 'THE BYTES ARE ONLY VALID FOR THE DURATION OF THE CALL', which under the three-argument overload is false for a dropped sink -- its call is still in progress while the array is overwritten. Not raised as major because the overload is unwired and M5.58 blocks wiring it, so no sink can reach the state today; it belongs in M5.58's row rather than in a fourth round here.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer-socket sink is written against SegmentSink's contract and copies nothing, relying on 'valid for the duration of the call'. Once M5.58 closes and the deadline overload is wired, that sink stalls, is cancelled at 200 ms, swallows or is slow to see the interrupt, and continues writing `buffer[0..length)` to its socket while the serving thread has already refilled the array with the NEXT chunk. The consumer receives a byte range that is neither its chunk nor a whole one. The sink is dropped and never completed, so nothing is presented as a segment -- which is why this is a documentation gap rather than a correctness defect -- but the author had no way to know the guarantee it read did not hold. Close it by adding the exception to SegmentSink's javadoc, or by naming it in M5.58's row as part of what wiring owes.
